candidates.statement: The information and recommendations provided in this guidance are intended to be broadly applicable to potential future emerging pathogens . This guidance applies to all stages of an outbreak and includes discussion about when appropriate validation may depend on the stage of the outbreak. Additionally, FDA recognizes that outbreaks inherently come with uncertainty and that recommended validation approaches should be adjusted for certain situations. For example, different considerations may be needed in certain situations, such as matters of national security .
candidates.context: diagnostic tests 3 intended to detect a pathogen (s) to aid in the diagnos is of a serious or life - threatening infectious disease or condition for which a n applicable 5 64 declaration has been issued . 4 The recommendations in this guidance apply to test data and information submitted in a pre - EUA 5 or an EUA request , or for a test offered as described in an applicable e nforcement discretion policy . This guidance does not address the EUA regulatory process; refer to “ Emergency Use Authorization of Medical Products and Related Authorities ” for additional information. In any outbreak, FDA continually monitors and assesses the testing landscape in the U.S. and will update its policies and recommendations as appropriate.

candidates.statement: Test manufacturers should consider which sections are applicable based on the stage of the outbreak , availability of validation materials , and the design and proposed indication for use of their test , among other considerations .
candidates.context: Due to differences across tests, including technology and indications for use, as well as different circumstances across outbreak s , some sections of this guidance may not be applicable to all tests. FDA generally will work interactively with the manufacturer during the development and review of an EUA request to help ensure appropriate validation of a test, particularly given potential changes in recommendations due to the changing circumstances of any outbreak. Test manufacturers may also refer to the mpox and COVID - 19 EUA templates on FDA’s website for additional examples of approaches taken during prior emergencies. 6

candidates.statement: A generic template entitled “ General IVD Emergency Use Authorization (EUA) Request /Pre - EUA Template” is made available through download from our website , 7 and it reflects FDA’s current thinking on data and information that should be submit ted in pre - EUAs and EUA requests . FDA may provide more tailored recommendations for tests for a specific outbreak through separate guidance or pathogen - specific templates, as appropriate .
candidates.context: IV. Availability of Template s FDA has found the use of templates to be beneficial during prior emergencies , for both manufacturers and FDA reviewers, to help facilitate the preparation and submission of pre - EUAs and EUA requests to FDA , and any resulting authorization. Templates should be viewed only as recommendations, and alternative approaches can be used unless specific regulatory or statutory requirements are cited. Additional templates may be added to our website . For example, FDA may provide updated templates as appropriate in the event of a specific outbreak.

candidates.statement: V. Validation Study Recommendations V alidation should objectively demonstrate that a finished device can consistently fulfil l defined user needs and its intended use . The validation recommendations discussed here reflect that the “may be effective ” standard for EUAs 8 provides for a lower level of evidence than the “ effectiveness ” standard that FDA uses for product approvals, 9 as discussed in the FDA guidance, “ Emergency Use Authorization of Medical Products and Related Authorities . ” As such, the validation should demonstrate that the device may be effective for its intended use and that the known and potential benefits of the device when used as intended outweigh the known and potential risks of the device. This guidance also reflec ts the understanding that, in rapidly developing or unexpected emergency circumstances, it may not be possible for a manufacturer to collect and/or provide all of the recommended data , including in the format suggested in a timely manner. In such cases, additional information may become available and/or FDA might request such information at a later date .

candidates.statement: Clinical Performance Evaluation A clinical performance evaluation is used to assess the accuracy of a test in detecting the analyte of interest, often through method comparison or comparison of test results to known positive and negative specimens. This type of study typically should characterize the performance of the device as it would be expected to perform in actual clinical use. The number of samples and the design of the study, such as an appropriate comparator method, will depend on many factors including the target pathogen, type of test, availability of clinical specimens contain ing the pathogen, availability of appropriate comparator methods, the stage of the outbreak, and overall testing needs.
candidates.context: Additionally, certain validation studies described in Section V and 0 may be applicable only for certain device types or technologies. FDA recommends that manufacturers consider the validation studies applicable to their device type, as discussed in subsections A and B . For example, for a viral nucleic acid test using established technologies known to be capable of high sensitivity detection, at a stage of the outbreak where clinical samples and comparators are generally available, at least 30 positive and 30 negative s pecimens (as defined by the comparator) from the intended use population and using the intended specimen type are typically adequate to demonstrate the performance of the test compared to a highly sensitive comparator method . Evaluation of fewer specimens may not accurately characterize the true performance of the test. 11

candidates.statement: However, in the early stages of an emerging disease outbreak, natural clinical specimens may not be readily available. In such cases, the use of archived positive and negative clinical specimens 12 could be a reasonable alternative. Ideally, archived specimens should be accompanied by information to determine sample adequacy, such as the specimen collection date, specimen storage conditions, and date of onset of symptoms.
candidates.context: (1) Initial Stages of the Outbreak - Alternative Specimen Types Natural clinical specimens are the preferred sample type for validation of a diagnostic test. When prospective and archived samples are not available, use of contrived (e.g., spiked) samples may be acceptable. Contrived samples are constructed in the laboratory by placing known concentrations of a microorganism or analyte into individual (not poole d) human specimens known to be negative for that microorganism or analyte (i.e., negative clinical matrix 13 ). In situations where pathogen stocks are not available, such as at the early stages of an outbreak , FDA would likely consider use of synthetic material to be acceptable . 14 When synthetic material is used, it should closely mimic natural materials . candidates.statement: 12 For purposes of this guidance, archived specimens, sometimes referred to as retrospective or banked specimens , are defined as specimens collected from a human subject that are known to harbor the analyte of interest (i.e., positive) or not harbor the analyte (i.e., negative). Archived samples should be selected to minimize bias; for instance, samples should not be selected for archiving based on the candidate test result . The appropriateness for use of archived samples, such as length of time in storage or other factors, will vary based on the individual emerging pathogen during an outbreak.

When a clinical performance evaluation is not a prospective study, FDA recommends that manufacturers ensure that their evaluation include s samples that appropriately represent the range of pathogen levels expected in clinical specimens in the intended use population. 13 For purposes of this guidance, clinical matrix is defined as a specimen taken from a human subject. Negative clinical matrix is a clinical specimen taken from a human subject which does not harbor the analyte of interest.

candidates.statement: (3) Clinical Data Analysis G enerally , a ll samples meeting pre - defined inclusion criteria for the clinical performance evaluation should be included in the analysis . J ustification should be provided for exclusion of any such samples from data analysis . FDA generally recommends that clinical data analysis include the calculation of positive percent agreement (PPA) and negative percent agreement (NPA) with a highly sensitive comparator method , and corresponding 95% confidence intervals using the Wilson Score method. Target PPA and NPA to support adequate performance of a diagnostic test depend on the test type and indications for use as well as a benefit/risk assessment in the context of the emerging outbreak . FDA may consider lower PPA s acceptable for different test types and intended use po pulations with certain mitigations , such as reporting of negative test results as “presumptive” based on benefit - risk considerations. I n certain cases, such as for screening tests for asymptomatic individuals, a higher NPA has generally be en expected . If the test is intended for symptomatic individuals, the data should include time from symptom onset to test for each enrolled subject . T he data analysis should account for performance shifts in relation to time from symptom onset to support adequate clinical performance .
candidates.context: Manufacturers should consult FDA prior to implementing enrichment approaches in your clinical performance evaluation . 15 For example, for respiratory viruses, examples of the most challenging clinical matrix type include nasopharyngeal (NP) swabs for common upper respiratory types or sputum for common lower respiratory types.

candidates.statement: (1) Limit of Detection (LoD) (Analytical Sensitivity) The LoD provides a measure of the analytical sensitivity of a test for a particular target analyte and is defined as the lowest concentration of target analyte that is consistently detected by the test in 95% of the specimen replicates . 18 The LoD results guide additional validation studies , including the clinical performance evaluation . LoD should be determined using the entire test from specimen preparation and extraction through detection and the result interpretation algorithm. In some cases, it may be appropriate to determine LoD only for the most challenging negative clinical matrix type included in the intended use of the device . For atypical specimen types, the LoD should be determined with each specimen type included in the intended use of the device .
candidates.context: 812) may be applicable to certain IVD clinical studies. candidates.statement: Generally, t he preliminary LoD is determined by testing a 2 - 3 - fold dilution series of three replicates per concentration. The lowest concentration at which all tested replicates are positive is considered the preliminary LoD. The preliminary LoD study should include at least one concentration that does not yield 100% positive results. The LoD should then be confirmed by testing a minimum of 20 individual replicates of the concentration determined to be the preliminary LoD. The final LoD is the lowest concentration resulting in positive detection of at least 95% of the replicates (e.g., at least 19 out of 2 0 replicates). In the case where the final LoD study achieves a positivity of 100%, a lower concentration (using a 3 - fold dilution) should be tested (with 20 replicates) until < 95% positivity is obtained. While the LoD for an entire analyte is most critical for test validation, FDA might also request the LoD for individual targets f or multi - target tests to help the Agency evaluate the performance of the device . 21 (2) Inclusivity (Analytical Reactivity) An inclusivity study show s reactivity of the test with additional related (e.g., tax onomic, immunological, and genetic composition) target species or isolates.

candidates.statement: I n clusivity of antigen - based tests should be evaluated through wet testing of currently circulating variants . The methods and results of this analysis should show the extent to which variation in the target genome may affect clinical and analytical sens itivity. FDA recommends monthly evaluation of inclusivity to account for new and emerging clinically significant mutations. This could include , for example, assessing the prevalence of mutations in well - established publicly available sequence databases and monitoring for credible reports that a given variant or mutation has the potential to increase pathogenicity , increase transmission, or otherwise increase the risk to public health. FDA might request additional testing based on its own monitoring . The aggregate impact of the mutations should be evaluated and should not result in the clinical performance point estimates for the test dropping below the clinical performance recommendations described in Section V.A . If a greater than 3 - fold reduction in analytical sensitivity is observed when comparing pathogen s with and without the mutation , manufacturers should conduct a risk analysis for the observed difference in performance , consider further risk mitigations, and assess whether the known and potential benefits of the test continue to outweigh the known and potential risks.

candidates.statement: (3) S pecimen Stability D egradation of a specimen prior to testing can lead to false results. T he Centers for Disease Control and Prevention ( CDC ) often communicate s acceptable specimen stability conditions for certain specimen types to be tested for specific analytes . 22 In such cases, when a manufacturer uses CDC ’s specifications for specimen stability, additional data are likely not needed to support validation. For a dditional or extended specimen stability conditions not supported by CDC’s specifications, or in cases where CDC has not communicated specifications, the manufacturer should validate their proposed specimen stability conditions in a specimen stability study , as described in this section .

candidates.statement: (6) Potential Additional Testing In addition to the recommended analytical validation discussed throughout this guidance, additional testing may be recommended in certain circumstances. Some examples are outlined briefly here: Antigen tests should generally be evaluated for high - dose hook effect, which occurs when the presence of very high levels of the target analyte in the patient specimen interferes with the binding ability of the capture antibody and causes false negative results. If the clinic al evaluation does not use real clinical specimens, then cross - reactivity, microbial interference, and endogenous/exogenous interference studies should generally be performed, typically with wet testing using the most sensitive extraction/instrument combination and the Limit of Detection (LoD) with the lowest an alyte concentration. FDA may also find it appropriate to request studies such as these in other circumstances where there may be a question or concern about accuracy or reliability , such as when novel approaches are used or where there are signals of potential impacts on test performance. Cross - reactivity should be evaluated to establish that the test does not react with related non - target microorganisms, high prevalence disease causing agents, and commensal or pathogenic flora that are likely to be in the clinical specimen . In addition, microbial interference should be evaluated to establish test performance when the target analyte is present in a clinical specimen with other relevant non - target microorganisms.

candidates.statement: Home Specimen Collection and Home Use Tests Home specimen collection and home use tests may be beneficial during a n outbreak by increas ing patient access to testing and by reducing potential exposure s . Home specimen collection involves the use of a home collection kit to collect a specimen and send it to a laboratory for testing . A home use test involves collecting a specimen and testing it at home, without needing to send it anywhere else. FDA recommends that manufacturers of home collection kits and home use tests consider incorporati ng design features to address user accessibility (e.g., for vision or hearing deficits). Home c ollection kits and home use tests should use only non - invasive specimen collection methods that require no specialized training to be safely and correctly performed . The home collection kit or home use test should be safe for home use and for lay - user collection of specimens from the intended anatomical site . Home collection kits and home use tests should be assessed for toxicology. Home collection kits or home use tests that contain hazardous materials may not be appropriate w ithout adequate risk mitigat ions such as safety features to limit the risk of patient exposure. candidates.statement: In general, a home use test should be simple to perform, and its results should be simple to interpret. Home use tests can be prescription use or over the counter (OTC) and can be used in non - laboratory settings, such as offices, sporting events, airports, schools, where a lay person collects a sample, performs the test , and interprets test results themselves . The clinical performance evaluation of home use tests should be conducted at U.S. sites representative of the intended use setting (i.e., that mimic a home use environment) and with users who represent the intended use population (e.g., including different socioeconomic and educational backgrounds and range of ages). Generally, for OTC tests, the intended use patient population includes adults (and older pediatric individuals ) who can perform self - collection and testing, pediatric individuals who may be able to self - collect and perform the test under supervision of an adult, and younger pediatric individuals (and some adults) who need their specimen collected and tested by an adult caregiver. Each patient population proposed should be evaluated following the validation recommendations discussed elsewhere in this guidance . The entire workflow should be performed by each individual participant including, as applicable, test registration, specimen collection, testing, and results interpretation. Testing sites should be set up in a way that precludes a user from seeing or hea ring other users performing the test (e.g., in separate rooms).

A manufacturer that has provided data to the FDA may grant a right of reference to other manufacturer s, either broadly or to individual manufacturer s. Point of Care (POC) Tests Point - of - Care (POC) test s are tests intended for use in professional near patient settings, such as hospitals, urgent care centers , and emergency rooms .

candidates.statement: Clinical performance evaluation of POC emergency use tests that are intended for use in a CLIA Certificate of Waiver setting should be conducted at one or two U.S. sites representative of anticipated real - world settings , with four to six operators without laboratory training , and who are representative of intended operators . For example, this may include : us ing the device in a healthcare setting, such as at a hospital bedside , by non - laboratorian healthcare professionals ; in a non - traditional healthcare setting , such as at a school , by untrained users who are not healthcare professionals ; or in a temporary testing site setting , s uch as a tent set up at a non - healthcare workplace, by users who have limited or no training or hands - on experience in conducting laboratory testing . The clinical performance evaluation for POC tests should include all steps in specimen collection and handling described in labeling , including addition of the specimen to the specimen port/well of the test . Testing should be performed in real time after specimen collection . Study o perators should only rely on QRI and should receive no additional training or intervention on how to use the device . The QRI should be written for untrained users at no higher than a 7th grade reading level , limited to one to two pages , and include pictures and diagrams to facilitate use.
candidates.context: Point of Care (POC) Tests Point - of - Care (POC) test s are tests intended for use in professional near patient settings, such as hospitals, urgent care centers , and emergency rooms . POC tests can be beneficial during an outbreak because they provide more immediate results compared to laboratory - based tests . In addition to the clinical performance evaluation described above in Section V.A , for POC tests , performance around the LoD should be evaluated by the intended POC users with contrived specimens in real clinical matrix . Testing should include 10 samples near the LoD (e.g., ≤ 3 - fold of the LoD) , and 10 negative specimens per site. All contrived specimens should be blinded, randomized, and tested as part of the normal workflow of the site by the intended POC users , each of whom test s at least three positive samples near the LoD and three negative samples.
